claims.sentence: Two independent compositions place יִבְצֹר רוּחַ נְגִידִים beside Isaiah 63's warrior מִבָּצְרָה... חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים, "crimsoned in garments from Bozrah" (Isa 63:1): the Ashkenazi Rosh Hashanah *yotzer* and a Hasidic Shabbat *zemer* that names both Edom and Bozrah (quoted in the liturgical section).
claims.claim: The named Rosh Hashanah yotzer and Shabbat zemer place יִבְצֹר רוּחַ נְגִידִים alongside Isaiah 63’s Edom/Bozrah and bloodied-garment language; the zemer names both Edom and Bozrah.

evidence.source: Research materials, Modern Jewish Liturgical Use: Rosh Hashanah yotzer
evidence.quote: מֶֽלֶךְ חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים. בְּדָרְכוֹ בוֹגְדִים. יִבְצֹר רֽוּחַ נְגִידִים

evidence.source: Research materials, Modern Jewish Liturgical Use: Shabbat zemer
evidence.quote: בְּבוֹאוֹ מֵאֱדוֹם חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים ... בְּבָצְרָה ... יִבְצוֹר רוּחַ נְגִידִים
מִי־זֶ֣ה ׀ בָּ֣א מֵאֱד֗וֹם חֲמ֤וּץ בְּגָדִים֙ מִבׇּצְרָ֔ה

claims.explanation: The liturgical material identifies the yotzer as Ashkenazic and the zemer as used in the Siddur Sefard tradition, including Hasidic communities; its quoted stanza includes both Edom and Bozrah. Isaiah 63:1 supplies the cited phrase.

claims.sentence: They were hearing a real cluster of shared language.
claims.claim: The following listed parallels are shared language between Isaiah 63 and Psalm 76.

evidence.quote: Isaiah 63:1: רַ֥ב לְהוֹשִֽׁיעַ; Psalm 76:10: לְהוֹשִׁ֖יעַ
Isaiah: חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים ... עַל־בְּגָדַ֔י; Psalm 76: תַּחְגֹּֽר
Isaiah 63:3: פּוּרָ֣ה ׀ דָּרַ֣כְתִּי ... כְּדֹרֵ֥ךְ בְּגַֽת; Psalm 76:13: יִ֭בְצֹר

claims.explanation: The verses share the cited Hebrew vocabulary and imagery: salvation, wrath/anger, clothing, and vintage imagery. The “cluster” is a summary of those verifiable parallels.

claims.sentence: - לְהוֹשִׁיעַ, "to save" (63:1; compare v. 10);
claims.claim: לְהוֹשִׁיעַ occurs in Isaiah 63:1 and Psalm 76:10.

evidence.quote: רַ֥ב לְהוֹשִֽׁיעַ׃
לְהוֹשִׁ֖יעַ כׇּל־עַנְוֵי־אֶ֣רֶץ

claims.explanation: Both verses contain the cited form.

claims.sentence: - repeated חֵמָה and אַף, "fury" and "anger" (63:3, 5, 6; compare vv. 8, 11);
claims.claim: Isaiah 63:3, 5, and 6 use forms of חֵמָה and אַף, and Psalm 76:8 and 11 use the corresponding fury/anger vocabulary.
claims.explanation: The listed verses contain the respective forms of חֵמָה and אַף.

claims.sentence: - clothing (compare the girding of v. 11);
claims.claim: Isaiah 63 uses clothing imagery that can be compared with Psalm 76:11’s girding language.

evidence.quote: חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים ... עַל־בְּגָדַ֔י ... וְכׇל־מַלְבּוּשַׁ֖י
שְׁאֵרִ֖ית חֵמֹ֣ת תַּחְגֹּֽר

claims.explanation: Isaiah names garments and clothing; Psalm 76:11 uses תַּחְגֹּר, from the girding vocabulary.

claims.sentence: - a winepress (compare the vintage here);
claims.claim: Isaiah 63:3 depicts treading a vintage in a press, while Psalm 76:13 uses a verb that Ibn Ezra relates to grape-harvesting.

evidence.quote: פּוּרָ֣ה ׀ דָּרַ֣כְתִּי לְבַדִּ֗י ... כְּדֹרֵ֥ךְ בְּגַֽת
יבצור - דרך משל כטעם יכרות מגזרת בציר

claims.explanation: The Isaiah verse uses vintage/press imagery, and Ibn Ezra connects יִבְצֹר figuratively with cutting from the grape-harvest root.

claims.sentence: - Edom, whose name sits one vowel from אָדָם in v. 11;
claims.claim: The name Edom differs from אָדָם by only one vowel.

evidence.quote: אֱדוֹם
אָדָם

claims.explanation: The names echo one another, but their Masoretic pronunciations differ in both vowel positions.
claims.suggested_fix: - Edom, whose name echoes אָדָם in v. 11;

claims.sentence: - above all, a victory with no human ally: וְאַבִּיט וְאֵין עֹזֵר, "I looked, and there was no one to help" (63:5).
claims.claim: Isaiah 63:5 says the speaker looked and found no one to help, presenting a victory without a human ally.

evidence.quote: וְאַבִּיט֙ וְאֵ֣ין עֹזֵ֔ר

claims.explanation: The verse says, “Then I looked, but there was none to help.” The quotation and the claim about the lack of a helper are supported.

claims.sentence: Radak's comment on this final verse is an admission: כבד במכלול בשרש חגר פירשתי זה המזמור על מחנה אשור כשבא על ירושלים, אבל עתה נראה לי לטעם המזמור אשר למעלה ממנו לפרש אותו על גוג מגוג, "In the *Mikhlol*, under the root חגר, I already explained this psalm as concerning the Assyrian camp when it came against Jerusalem; but now, given the sense of the psalm that precedes it, it seems to me it should be explained of Gog and Magog."
claims.claim: The Hebrew quotation and its attribution to Radak on Psalm 76:13 are accurate, and the English translation fairly represents it.

evidence.quote: כבר במכלול בשרש חגר פירשתי זה המזמור על מחנה אשור כשבא על ירושלים, אבל עתה נראה לי לטעם המזמור אשר למעלה ממנו לפרש אותו על גוג מגוג

claims.explanation: The quoted Hebrew matches Radak’s entry. The English accurately conveys his earlier Assyrian interpretation and his present inclination to read the psalm as concerning Gog and Magog because of the preceding psalm.

claims.sentence: The great grammarian changed his mind in print and left the earlier view in his own grammar book, where a reader looking up "gird" would still find Sennacherib.
claims.claim: Radak reports an earlier Assyrian reading in his Mikhlol under the root חגר and contrasts it with his later Gog-and-Magog reading.

evidence.quote: במכלול בשרש חגר פירשתי זה המזמור על מחנה אשור כשבא על ירושלים, אבל עתה נראה לי ... לפרש אותו על גוג מגוג

claims.explanation: Radak explicitly identifies his earlier explanation as being in the Mikhlol under חגר and states that he now sees the psalm as concerning Gog and Magog. The supplied entry does not independently establish how a reader would locate the discussion in the grammar book.

claims.sentence: His reason was sequence.
claims.claim: Radak gives the preceding psalm as the reason for his changed interpretation.

evidence.quote: לטעם המזמור אשר למעלה ממנו

claims.explanation: Radak says his revised reading follows from the sense of the psalm above it.

claims.sentence: Psalm 75 promises a coming judgment, so Psalm 76, he reasoned, must describe it.
claims.claim: Psalm 75 speaks of God’s coming judgment, and Radak relates his Gog-and-Magog reading of Psalm 76 to the preceding psalm.

evidence.quote: כִּ֭י אֶקַּ֣ח מוֹעֵ֑ד ... אֶשְׁפֹּֽט׃ ... כִּ֤י אֱלֹהִ֥ים שֹׁפֵ֑ט
לטעם המזמור אשר למעלה ממנו לפרש אותו על גוג מגוג

claims.explanation: Psalm 75 describes God judging, and Radak expressly cites the preceding psalm as a reason for reading Psalm 76 as concerning Gog and Magog. “Must” is a summary of the inference rather than Radak’s wording.

claims.sentence: His new reading cost him the forced future tense of v. 3's "and it was."
claims.claim: Radak renders Psalm 76:3’s וַיְהִי as a future event in his Gog-and-Magog reading.

evidence.quote: ויהי. ואז יהיה בשלם בסכה

claims.explanation: Radak glosses וַיְהִי with ואז יהיה (“then it will be”), reading the event as future. Calling this rendering “forced” is an evaluation, not a separate checkable fact.

claims.sentence: The poem's own tenses explain his dilemma.
claims.claim: The psalm’s tense pattern is relevant to the contrast between a past-event reading and a future reading.

evidence.quote: תּוֹדֶךָּ ... תַּחְגֹּר ... יֹבִילוּ ... יִבְצֹר

claims.explanation: The narrative portion includes past-oriented forms, while the closing section uses imperfect forms and imperatives that can be read prospectively. This is a broad description of the pattern, not a claim that every form in verses 3–10 is past tense.

claims.sentence: The past-tense story of vv. 3–10 supports the Assyrian reading; the future-tense coda supports Gog.
claims.claim: The narrative and closing verbal forms can be read as supporting historical and future interpretations, respectively.

evidence.quote: תּוֹדֶךָּ ... תַּחְגֹּר ... יֹבִילוּ ... יִבְצֹר
לפרש אותו על גוג מגוג

claims.explanation: The contrast is a defensible account of the poem’s narrative past-oriented forms and the coda’s imperfect forms. It should not be taken to mean every verb in verses 3–10 is past tense.

claims.sentence: Meiri, facing the same fork, lets the reciter choose: the speaker, he says, may interpret it as he wishes.
claims.claim: Meiri leaves the Assyrian and Gog-and-Magog readings as equally open choices for the speaker.

evidence.quote: ויתכן לפרשו על מלחמת גוג ומגוג לעתיד והוא הנכון לסמיכותו למזמור שלפניו יפרשם המדבר כרצונו

claims.explanation: Meiri prefers the Gog-and-Magog reading but explicitly says the speaker may interpret it as he wishes; the sentence reports that latitude without claiming equal preference.

claims.sentence: The poem's frame now closes.
claims.claim: The following sentence identifies the psalm’s opening and closing phrases.

evidence.quote: נוֹדָע בִּיהוּדָה
נוֹרָא לְמַלְכֵי־אָרֶץ

claims.explanation: The cited phrases appear at the beginning and end of the psalm’s body.

claims.sentence: It opened with נוֹדָע בִּיהוּדָה, "known in Judah," and closes with נוֹרָא לְמַלְכֵי־אָרֶץ, "awesome to the kings of the earth."
claims.claim: Psalm 76:2 contains נוֹדָע בִּיהוּדָה, and Psalm 76:13 contains נוֹרָא לְמַלְכֵי־אָרֶץ, with the supplied English glosses.

evidence.quote: נוֹדָ֣ע בִּיהוּדָ֣ה
נ֝וֹרָ֗א לְמַלְכֵי־אָֽרֶץ

claims.explanation: Both Hebrew phrases and their general English senses are supported by the verses.

claims.sentence: The two words differ by a single letter, ד against ר, and the distance between them is the whole psalm's widening from one tribe to the world.
claims.claim: נוֹדָע and נוֹרָא differ by only one letter, ד versus ר.

evidence.quote: נוֹדָע
נוֹרָא

claims.explanation: The words differ in two letters: ד/ר and ע/א.
claims.suggested_fix: The two words differ by two letters, ד against ר and ע against א, and the distance between them is the whole psalm's widening from one tribe to the world.

claims.sentence: The last word is אָרֶץ, "earth," its third appearance in five verses.
claims.claim: The last word of Psalm 76 is אָרֶץ, which occurs three times in the final five verses, 9–13.

evidence.quote: אֶ֖רֶץ ... עַנְוֵי־אֶ֣רֶץ ... לְמַלְכֵי־אָֽרֶץ

claims.explanation: The word occurs in verses 9, 10, and 13 of the final five verses; verse 13 ends with אָרֶץ.

claims.sentence: One documented scene shows what happens when this poem enters a human mouth.
claims.claim: The specific historical scene described below is documented.
claims.explanation: The purported scene is not included in the supplied claims. Without its people, event, or source, a search cannot establish whether that specific scene is documented.

claims.sentence: On 1 June 1679, an outlawed field-meeting of Scottish Covenanters near Loudoun Hill saw government dragoons under John Graham of Claverhouse riding toward them.
claims.claim: The date, location, status of the meeting, identity of the opposing force and commander, and their approach are accurate historical details.

evidence.source: Historic Environment Scotland, Battle of Drumclog.
evidence.quote: Arriving at Drumclog on 1 June 1679, having heard that a conventicle was taking place, John Graham of Claverhouse ... found an armed force of Covenanters

evidence.source: Scottish Covenanter Memorials Association, Battle of Drumclog. ([covenanter.org.uk](https://www.covenanter.org.uk/drumclog_battle.html))
evidence.quote: Claverhouse ... attacked a large Conventicle being held at Drumclog

claims.explanation: The battle record identifies the date, conventicle, Covenanters and Claverhouse; the meeting was near Loudoun Hill. The description of the dragoons approaching fairly summarizes the encounter.

claims.sentence: Covenanter tradition remembers that before engaging, they sang Psalm 76 in the Scottish metrical version:
claims.claim: Covenanter tradition records Psalm 76 being sung before battle in a Scottish metrical version.

evidence.source: Research materials, Deep Web Research: Battle Hymns & Anti-Tyranny Movements
evidence.quote: Scottish Covenanters sang Robert Pont’s metrical Psalm 76 prior to battle (e.g., Battle of Drumclog, 1679).

claims.explanation: The research materials document this general Covenanter practice and its association with Drumclog. The specific Loudoun Hill scene is not established by that summary.

claims.sentence: Covenanter tradition remembers that before engaging, they sang Psalm 76 in the Scottish metrical version:
claims.claim: The four quoted lines are an accurate quotation from the Scottish metrical version of Psalm 76.

evidence.source: Scottish Metrical Psalter (1650), Psalm 76, reproduced by iPsalm. ([ipsalm.nl](https://ipsalm.nl/en/psalm/76/Scottish1650))
evidence.quote: By him the sp’rits shall be cut off
In particular they sang Psalm 76

claims.explanation: An account supports the tradition that they sang Psalm 76, and the metrical text is available. But the four lines to be checked are not included in the material supplied, so their accuracy cannot be verified.

claims.sentence: Then they charged and routed the dragoons.
claims.claim: The Covenanters charged and routed the dragoons in the described encounter.

evidence.source: Historic Environment Scotland, Battle of Drumclog.
evidence.quote: the whole of the Covenanter force charged ... the government troops ... were overwhelmed and fled

claims.explanation: The recorded charge and flight support both parts of the sentence.

claims.sentence: For these men, persecuted by a king who claimed authority over their church, the psalm's promise that God "prunes the spirit of princes" was a political creed.
claims.claim: The Covenanters in this scene were persecuted by a king who claimed authority over their church.

evidence.source: National Museums Scotland, Alexander Peden: The masked preacher. ([nms.ac.uk](https://www.nms.ac.uk/discover-catalogue/alexander-peden-the-masked-preacher))
evidence.quote: the new King ... declared himself the head of the Scottish kirk ... A period of persecution followed
the Covenanters ... believed only Jesus Christ and God could sit at the head of the Church

claims.explanation: The king was Charles II. The sources substantiate both royal claims over the Scottish kirk and the persecution of Covenanters.

claims.sentence: They sang a poem in which no human being fights, and then they fought.
claims.claim: Psalm 76 narrates no human being fighting, and the Covenanters then fought in the described incident.

evidence.quote: שָׁמָּה שִׁבַּר רִשְׁפֵי־קָשֶׁת ... וְלֹא־מָצְאוּ כָל־אַנְשֵׁי־חַיִל יְדֵיהֶם
they sang Psalm 76 ... through the bog and amongst them

claims.explanation: The psalm credits the breaking of weapons to God and describes warriors unable to use their hands; it narrates no human combatant fighting. An account of Drumclog describes the Covenanters singing the psalm and then engaging the dragoons.

claims.sentence: Every community that has sung Psalm 76 has done what Rashi and Radak did on paper: supplied the missing "we."
claims.claim: Every community that has sung Psalm 76 has supplied an implied first-person “we.”

evidence.source: Scottish Metrical Psalter (1650), Psalm 76, reproduced by iPsalm. ([ipsalm.nl](https://ipsalm.nl/en/psalm/76/Scottish1650))
evidence.quote: In Judah’s land God is well known

claims.explanation: A sung text establishes what a community could sing, not whether its singers supplied an implied first-person voice. The evidence does not establish this claim about every community.

claims.sentence: The psalm itself never does.
claims.claim: Psalm 76 contains no first-person form referring to an “I” or “we.”

evidence.quote: The body uses third-person and second-person forms; verse 12 addresses a plural audience with נִדְרוּ וְשַׁלְּמוּ and אֱלֹהֵיכֶם.

claims.explanation: The psalm’s body contains no first-person pronoun or first-person verb form; the direct plural address appears in verse 12.
